meta.title: Interwoven
meta.description: How science and technology build on one another
meta.provenance: Generated from research/science-technology-graph. Do not edit by hand.

nodes.title: B-DNA helical constraints
nodes.date_basis: This node is the qualified interpretation documented in the account signed 2 April 1953, not the earlier photographic exposure.
nodes.summary: Franklin and Gosling inferred a probable helix, approximately 34 Å repeat and 20 Å diameter, with exterior phosphates and a probable two-chain unit.
nodes.uncertainty: The authors did not call diffraction alone direct proof of helicity or offer a complete structure; the model involved additional density and chemical arguments.

nodes.title: Chain-termination DNA sequencing
nodes.date_basis: Method demonstrated by contribution on 3 October 1977; December publication is a later report milestone.
nodes.summary: Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson generated base-specific terminated extension products using nucleotide analogues and read the size-separated products on gels.
regions: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, England
nodes.uncertainty: The paper used both dideoxy and arabino analogues and credited earlier inhibitor chemistry; it is not credited with the first φX174 genome report.

nodes.title: DNA double-helix model
nodes.date_basis: Proposed structural model in the manuscript signed 2 April 1953; date belongs to model proposal, not discovery of DNA.
nodes.summary: Watson and Crick proposed antiparallel helical chains with complementary A–T and G–C pairs, drawing on chemical constraints and others’ experimental work.
nodes.uncertainty: The paper explicitly treats the model as unproved. Donohue, Franklin, Gosling, Wilkins, other King’s workers and prior chemical researchers are not collapsed into sole-person credit.

nodes.title: DNA polymerase preparation
nodes.date_basis: Detailed purification/assay work was submitted 10 October 1957 and published in 1958; this is a by-date, not a first-discovery claim.
nodes.summary: Lehman, Bessman, Simms and Kornberg prepared substrates, partially purified an E. coli DNA polymerase and assayed DNA incorporation.
regions: Washington University, St. Louis, Missouri, USA
nodes.uncertainty: Partial purification is not a pure modern reagent. The authors’ rationale came from coenzyme chemistry; no double-helix-to-enzyme invention edge is claimed.

nodes.title: Four-colour primer readout
nodes.date_basis: The demonstrated system was submitted 30 December 1985 and described in June 1986; interval avoids treating the journal date as invention day.
nodes.summary: Smith and colleagues tagged primers with four fluorophores, combined reaction products in one gel tube and acquired detected bands by computer.
regions: Applied Biosystems, Foster City, California, USA
nodes.uncertainty: Partial automation, not an autonomous genome factory; the inspected abstract does not establish a commercial launch date.

nodes.title: Fluorescent terminator sequencing
nodes.date_basis: Demonstrated M13 sequencing system described on 16 October 1987; earlier construction date not resolved in the abstract.
nodes.summary: Prober and colleagues combined four dye-labelled dideoxy terminators with reverse transcriptase, one reaction mixture, electrophoresis and automated sequence calls.
nodes.uncertainty: Abstract-level access; no claim that this exact reagent set or enzyme was used unchanged by all Human Genome Project centres.

nodes.title: Human genome draft
nodes.date_basis: Anchored to the 7 October 2000 data snapshot analysed in the February 2001 paper.
nodes.summary: The public consortium’s assembled draft provided broad human genome sequence coverage while retaining gaps and ambiguities.
nodes.uncertainty: Not a gapless genome, an inventory of every human variant, or proof that all reported gene-count interpretations remained correct.

nodes.title: Mapped-clone genome sequencing
nodes.date_basis: Dates the public consortium’s production phase and procedures used for the October 2000 draft, not invention of shotgun sequencing.
nodes.summary: The public consortium sequenced mapped BAC/PAC clones with automated fluorescent reads and computational assembly.
nodes.uncertainty: This node is the public consortium configuration, not Celera’s whole-genome strategy or every possible way to assemble a genome.

nodes.title: Humidity-varied DNA diffraction
nodes.date_basis: Archive dates the original B-form image to 1952; the humidity-dependent procedure is documented by the signed 2 April 1953 account.
nodes.summary: Franklin and Gosling obtained DNA-fibre X-ray patterns under differing hydration, distinguishing crystalline A and wetter B configurations.
nodes.uncertainty: No claim of inventing X-ray diffraction or DNA diffraction; exact instrument construction is not reconstructed here.

nodes.title: Viral DNA base ratios
nodes.date_basis: Measurements were reported in a manuscript received 1 July 1952; bounded as established by that year, without claiming the earliest such measurements.
nodes.summary: Wyatt’s analyses of DNA from 11 insect viruses found A:T and G:C near unity while aggregate base composition varied.
nodes.uncertainty: Not the origin of all base-ratio work: Wyatt explicitly builds on earlier analyses; Chargaff’s broader programme remains to be expanded.

nodes.title: φX174 sequence report
nodes.date_basis: Node is the public sequence report of 24 February 1977; exact completion of all contributing experiments is not established by the inspected abstract.
nodes.summary: A reported approximately 5,375-nucleotide φX174 sequence, obtained with plus/minus sequencing, revealed overlapping coding regions.
regions: Cambridge, England; wider collaborating laboratories unresolved
nodes.uncertainty: This is the original approximate-length report, not the later corrected reference sequence; no universal first-genome claim.

nodes.title: Plus/minus DNA sequencing
nodes.date_basis: Demonstrations appear in a manuscript received 20 December 1974; publication followed in May 1975.
nodes.summary: Sanger and Coulson used primed DNA synthesis, limiting nucleotide conditions, E. coli and T4 polymerases, and gel separation to infer sequences.
regions: MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology, Cambridge, England
nodes.uncertainty: Not the first DNA sequencing attempt; earlier primed sequencing and synthetic-primer work are explicitly mentioned by the paper and remain backlog.

nodes.title: Template-directed DNA synthesis
nodes.date_basis: The 1959 lecture synthesizes the 1958 cited enzyme studies and then-current template evidence; interval marks that evidence/interpretation stage.
nodes.summary: Kornberg’s team interpreted DNA-dependent enzymatic synthesis as copying through complementary base pairing and presented several experimental lines of support.
nodes.uncertainty: A contemporary participant’s synthesis. It does not establish that the isolated reaction reproduced every step of cellular chromosome replication.

nodes.title: Parallel-current attraction and repulsion
nodes.date_basis: Composite memoir read 2 October includes communications of 18 and 25 September; exact experimental day not recovered.
nodes.summary: Two parallel straight conductor sections, one counterweighted and movable, carry currents from two voltaic piles; same-direction currents attract and opposite-direction currents repel.
nodes.uncertainty: The available English translation is modern and unattributed. No modern mathematical force law or exact September demonstration day is ascribed to this node.

nodes.title: Insulated-gate MOS transistor
nodes.date_basis: Museum narrative dates successful fabrication to 1959; the 1960 meeting report is corroborated by Moore’s account.
nodes.summary: Atalla and Kahng demonstrated a silicon field-effect transistor with an oxide-insulated gate controlling conduction between source and drain.
regions: Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States
nodes.uncertainty: Interval distinguishes fabrication from reporting. Cached Kahng US3102230 describes a particular bias arrangement and is not used as interchangeable proof of every conventional MOSFET detail.

nodes.title: Surface-state hypothesis
nodes.date_basis: Museum dates the proposal one year after the April 1945 experiment; the contemporary paper appeared in May 1947.
nodes.summary: Bardeen proposed that electronic states at a semiconductor surface could screen an applied field; his published contact model included surface charge and space charge.
regions: Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States
nodes.uncertainty: Conception year is retrospective; the abstract does not supply a day or establish a complete transistor theory.

nodes.title: Metal-filings contact detector
nodes.date_basis: Museum dates the filings device to about 1890; interval encodes that approximate attribution, not measured calendar bounds.
nodes.summary: A granular metallic-contact device whose conductivity changes under electrical disturbance; this filings device is the predecessor Marconi calls a Branly coherer.
nodes.uncertainty: The 1890 original paper has not yet been inspected; museum retrospective dating is the present boundary. The 1900–1910 tripod object is not represented here, and Branly is not credited with the later complete communication system.

nodes.title: Junction-isolated planar flip-flop
nodes.date_basis: Working boron-diffused isolation circuits dated 27 September; public Micrologic announcement followed March 1961.
nodes.summary: Haas and Kattner’s boron-diffusion isolation process produced working flip-flop circuits using p–n junction separation.
nodes.uncertainty: This is not the claim that all integrated circuits require p–n junction isolation.

nodes.title: Physically isolated planar flip-flop
nodes.date_basis: Working monolithic devices dated 26 May by the museum; not the 1961 public announcement.
nodes.summary: Jay Last’s team made the Norman flip-flop using rear-etched channels filled with insulating epoxy to separate circuit components.
nodes.uncertainty: Exact day comes from retrospective history; original fabrication notebook remains a retrieval gap.

nodes.title: Silicon-gate 3708 multiplexer
nodes.date_basis: Commercial 3708 introduction in 1968; abbreviated technical presentation in October 1968, full paper in 1970.
nodes.summary: Faggin and Klein brought polysilicon-gate processing to ICs; Faggin redesigned an eight-channel analog multiplexer as the Fairchild 3708.
nodes.uncertainty: Not the origin of every self-aligned-gate idea: Bell Labs and Watkins antecedents are acknowledged as next-depth gaps.

nodes.title: Rotating copper-disc generator
nodes.date_basis: Working generator described in First Series read 24 November 1831; specific October dates are not asserted.
nodes.summary: A rotating copper disc passes between concentrated magnetic poles; sliding collectors at rim and axle feed a galvanometer, sustaining a deflection while rotation continues.
nodes.uncertainty: Experimental generator only. Collector irregularity and speed variation limited early readings; no claim of industrial power or direct ancestry of every later generator.

nodes.title: Moving-magnet induction test
nodes.date_basis: First Series read 24 November 1831 reports the performed test; no exact day inferred from paragraph order.
nodes.summary: A cylindrical permanent magnet is inserted into and withdrawn from a hollow coil connected to a galvanometer; motion gives opposite current impulses, and a stationary magnet gives none.
nodes.uncertainty: The account is not in strict chronological order. No battery is required as the inducing source in this particular configuration; magnet preparation is outside the claim.

nodes.title: Switching induces a second current
nodes.date_basis: Museum dates successful ring experiment to 29 August 1831; First Series gives the experimental configuration.
nodes.summary: Separately insulated windings around an iron ring connect to a battery and a remote galvanometer. Making or breaking the battery circuit gives opposite transient responses; steady current gives no sustained deflection.
nodes.uncertainty: This is an experimental result, not the later mathematical flux law or an efficient power transformer. The report deliberately rearranged experiments for exposition.

nodes.title: Mercury-contact electromagnetic rotation
nodes.date_basis: Diary entries for 3 and 4 September 1821 quoted by the Royal Institution.
nodes.summary: A battery-fed wire maintains contact through mercury while moving continuously around a magnetic pole; the following day’s arrangement improves wire and magnet support.
nodes.uncertainty: No claim of commercial usefulness or universal invention priority. The surviving 1822 object must not be used as an unqualified 1821 artifact.

nodes.title: Dielectric induction test proposed
nodes.date_basis: Hertz’s retrospective introduction dates the Berlin Academy prize problem to 1879.
nodes.summary: A proposed experiment seeks a relation between dielectric polarization and electromagnetic force, testing assumptions that connect Helmholtz’s electrodynamics to Maxwell’s equations.
nodes.uncertainty: A research programme, not an observed effect. Attribution of the problem’s precise theoretical motivation is Hertz’s later reconstruction; the Academy’s original announcement was not retrieved.

nodes.title: Reflected electrical waves in air
nodes.date_basis: Follows the November 1887 dielectric work and is reported in the 1888 air-wave paper; this interval avoids equating publication year with an unverified exact performance date.
nodes.summary: A spark oscillator illuminates a metal reflecting wall; moving and turning a spark-gap loop detects spatial strengthening and weakening consistent with incident/reflected waves.
nodes.uncertainty: Qualitative reflection/wave behavior only. Hertz later rejected the reliability of the air-versus-wire velocity comparison because of room/resonance effects; no precise light-speed measurement is claimed.

nodes.title: Fast spark oscillator and receiver
nodes.date_basis: Hertz dates the triggering observation to spring 1886 and the dielectric-test result to 10 November 1887.
nodes.summary: Induction-coil-driven spark oscillators and nearly closed secondary conductors with small adjustable gaps reveal rapid electrical oscillations; conductor placement is revised for dielectric tests.
nodes.uncertainty: Not a radio communication system. Initial spark discovery was contingent; Hertz explicitly says an essential spark property could not have been foreseen by theory.

nodes.title: Retained-oxide planar conception
nodes.date_basis: Notebook conception dated December 1957 by the museum; not yet a working transistor.
nodes.summary: Hoerni proposed leaving oxide over the junction edges while opening contact areas, instead of stripping the oxide after diffusion.
nodes.uncertainty: The original notebook itself was not inspected; date rests on the institutional account.

nodes.title: Working planar silicon transistor
nodes.date_basis: Working device dated March 1959; patent filed May 1959; commercial 2N1613 came in 1960.
nodes.summary: Hoerni implemented a silicon transistor whose diffused junction edges remained protected by oxide, with patterned contact openings.
nodes.uncertainty: Patent publication in 1962 is not the event date. Claimed ideal protection is not presented as measured universal reliability.

nodes.title: Intel 4004 CPU
nodes.date_basis: Working/commercial CPU implementation dated 1971 in the museum history.
nodes.summary: The MCS-4 family’s CPU function was implemented on the 4004 silicon-gate chip; Hoff and Mazor developed the architecture and Faggin with Shima implemented the design.
regions: Intel, California, United States; Busicom collaboration, Japan
nodes.uncertainty: A CPU chip, not a complete single-chip computer; peripheral chips remained part of MCS-4. No universal priority claim over all processor definitions.

nodes.title: Kilby germanium solid circuit
nodes.date_basis: Museum dates the working oscillator to 12 September 1958.
nodes.summary: Kilby connected germanium transistor, capacitor and resistor elements with fine gold wires to make an oscillator.
nodes.uncertainty: Museum caption calls this a multi-chip oscillator. It is not labelled a monolithic silicon IC; later TI flip-flops require separate nodes.

nodes.title: Aerial-and-earth wireless apparatus
nodes.date_basis: Marconi retrospectively dates the new arrangement to August 1895.
nodes.summary: One oscillator terminal connects to earth and the other to an elevated conductor; the receiver similarly connects its coherer between earth and an elevated conductor. Telegraph key, relay and tapping receiver apparatus support signs.
nodes.uncertainty: 1895 configuration and date rely on a 1909 participant account. This node does not establish exclusive priority, universal obstacle penetration or the necessity of earth connection for all radio systems.

nodes.title: Hertz–Branly signal trials
nodes.date_basis: Marconi’s 1909 lecture dates the initial home experiments to early 1895.
nodes.summary: An ordinary Hertz oscillator and Branly coherer are combined in preliminary tests aimed at transmitting telegraphic signs without connecting wires.
nodes.uncertainty: Retrospective participant testimony. The early Branly detector is described as unreliable; no generic 1895 radio-invention or performance claim is inferred.

nodes.title: Electromagnetic wave field theory
nodes.date_basis: Received 27 October and read 8 December 1864; expanded paper published 1865.
nodes.summary: A dynamical field formulation incorporates induction and electric displacement, yielding transverse disturbances with a calculated speed compared with optical measurements.
nodes.uncertainty: The 1864 framework uses a mechanical medium and twenty equations; it is not identical to the modern four-equation notation. Only the contemporary abstract and archival dating were inspected.

nodes.title: Metal-over-oxide IC conception
nodes.date_basis: Concept developed in 1959 and disclosed in the application filed 30 July; not a working chip at filing.
nodes.summary: Noyce proposed deposited metal conductors crossing retained oxide to connect semiconductor regions without shorting junctions, including multi-device circuits.
nodes.uncertainty: No Kilby-to-Noyce transmission is claimed. This patent’s isolation configuration must not be silently equated with every later junction-isolated IC.

nodes.title: Current deflects a needle
nodes.date_basis: Repeated observations reported by 21 July 1820; day of initial discovery is not assigned.
nodes.summary: A wire closing a galvanic circuit deflects a nearby suspended magnetic needle; moving the wire above/below reverses deflection; nonmagnetic needles provide controls.
nodes.uncertainty: The reported circular electrical-conflict explanation is historical. No claim that all magnetic phenomena or modern field theory were established in this experiment.

nodes.title: Ørsted’s twenty-trough battery
nodes.date_basis: Working apparatus specified in the report signed 21 July 1820.
nodes.summary: Twenty copper troughs with copper connections supporting zinc plates in the next trough; water with sulfuric and nitric acids; sufficient current for the closed-wire needle experiment.
nodes.uncertainty: This is the 1820 experimental battery, not a claim to its invention or manufacture by Ørsted. A smaller sufficiently strong apparatus was also said to work.

nodes.title: Silicon oxide diffusion mask
nodes.date_basis: Experimental development in 1955; patent/publication followed in 1957.
nodes.summary: Frosch and Derick used silicon dioxide to protect wafers and delimit dopant diffusion through etched openings.
regions: Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States
nodes.uncertainty: Masking depends on dopant and process conditions; no absolute impermeability to every dopant is asserted.

nodes.title: Oxide-stabilized silicon surfaces
nodes.date_basis: A 1958 ECS report is discussed in the Moore/Last oral history; the full experimental paper was received January 1959 and published May 1959.
nodes.summary: Atalla, Tannenbaum and Scheibner measured thermally oxidized silicon interfaces and device behavior, finding stable surface potentials with characteristic interface states.
regions: Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States
nodes.uncertainty: The report explicitly rejects universal applicability. Stability is not elimination of every surface state; exact first experimental date remains unresolved.

nodes.title: Photolithographic diffusion windows
nodes.date_basis: Museum dates Andrus and Bond’s adaptation to 1955; patent filing and later refinements are separate.
nodes.summary: Jules Andrus and Walter Bond adapted photoresist patterning to etch windows in silicon oxide before localized diffusion.
regions: Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States
nodes.uncertainty: This node is not Fairchild’s later step-and-repeat camera or DOFL’s separate diode-array work.

nodes.title: Germanium point-contact amplifier
nodes.date_basis: Successful amplification on 16 December; demonstration to laboratory officials on 23 December, as dated by the museum.
nodes.summary: Bardeen and Brattain placed two closely spaced gold contacts against germanium to obtain amplification.
regions: Bell Laboratories, New Jersey, United States
nodes.uncertainty: Not a silicon planar device; later transistor families are not attached by generic ancestry.

nodes.title: Volta’s series batteries
nodes.date_basis: Dated description of working configurations in the report read 26 June 1800; not a claim that construction began that day.
nodes.summary: Repeated silver–zinc pairs with saline-wetted separators in a column; an explicitly described alternative connected dissimilar-metal bows through a chain of liquid-filled cups.
nodes.uncertainty: The accessed source is the Royal Society’s 1832 abstract, not the full 1800 French paper. Earlier construction dates and the later trough-battery design genealogy remain outside this node.

nodes.title: Fairchild 2N1613 planar transistor
nodes.date_basis: IEEE historian reports Fairchild sold its first planar transistor, type 2N1613, in this month.
nodes.summary: Fairchild 2N1613, NPN diffused-silicon planar transistor; not all later 2N1613 manufacturers or variants.
nodes.uncertainty: April is an explicitly reported sale month; the first transaction day and any earlier limited pre-release offer were not independently established.

nodes.title: Fairchild physically isolated Micrologic flip-flop, early sample
nodes.date_basis: Jay Last reports first working physically isolated Micrologic devices in May.
nodes.summary: Four-transistor flip-flop on a monolithic chip with physical isolation, first functional version in May 1960; not necessarily identical to later production die.
nodes.uncertainty: Jay Last later recalled that first evaluation lots may have been physically isolated, but qualified the recollection.

nodes.title: Fairchild Micrologic Type F flip-flop
nodes.date_basis: Introduced in March and contemporary 29/31 March reports identify paid evaluation sales and an offer.
nodes.summary: Fairchild Micrologic Type F integrated flip-flop, 1961 introductory evaluation product; isolation process of earliest sold samples unconfirmed.
nodes.uncertainty: March 1961 applies to first reported commercial evaluation offer, not to every Micrologic family part or later junction-isolated production die.

nodes.title: Arelate supply aqueduct
nodes.date_basis: The 2018 site account states this interval of city-supply use; original construction is not independently dated.
nodes.summary: Southern spring-fed aqueduct branch supplying Arelate before diversion to Barbegal.
nodes.uncertainty: Chronology is inherited archaeological synthesis; the branch is not the whole Arelate water system.

nodes.title: Barbegal mill complex
nodes.date_basis: The 2018 site account dates diversion to the new mills around 120–130; the 2024 account retains a second-century placement.
nodes.summary: Two rows of eight watermills supplied by the redirected southern aqueduct branch.
nodes.uncertainty: Wooden wheels are lost. Exact housing, output and customer reconstructions are outside this node.

nodes.title: Alternating reusable forms
nodes.date_basis: Shen Gua retrospectively attributes the reported workflow to the Qingli reign; anchor is only a display midpoint.
nodes.summary: Two forms alternate composition and printing; reheating releases characters for storage and reuse.
nodes.uncertainty: One narrator’s process account. No print-run, labour, cost or later uptake inference.

nodes.title: Assembled iron-plate form
nodes.date_basis: Shen Gua retrospectively attributes the reported workflow to the Qingli reign; anchor is only a display midpoint.
nodes.summary: Fired types composed within a frame on a coated iron plate, warmed and leveled.
nodes.uncertainty: Same reported workflow as fired type; not an independently dated second invention.

nodes.title: Fired clay type
nodes.date_basis: Shen Gua retrospectively attributes the reported workflow to the Qingli reign; anchor is only a display midpoint.
nodes.summary: Bi Sheng’s separately carved clay characters, hardened by firing, as reported by Shen Gua.
nodes.uncertainty: Textual testimony; clay composition and physical performance remain unverified here.

nodes.title: Dholavira reservoirs
nodes.date_basis: ICOMOS assigns the reservoir expansion to archaeological Stage III; midpoint is display placement, not a dated year.
nodes.summary: Reservoirs east, south and west of the Castle, constructed during the Stage III urban expansion.
regions: Harappan South Asia; present-day Gujarat, India
nodes.uncertainty: The interval dates a construction phase; it does not establish the exact age of every drain or later repair.

nodes.title: Diamond Sutra scroll
nodes.date_basis: The artifact’s colophon is converted by its custodian to 11 May 868.
nodes.summary: Seven woodblock-printed paper sheets joined into a scroll; the custodian identifies hemp and mulberry paper.
regions: Found at Dunhuang, China; production site unspecified here
nodes.uncertainty: A surviving dated copy, not the invention of printing or paper. Findspot does not fix the printing workshop.

nodes.title: Hōkūleʻa built
nodes.date_basis: PVS voyage timeline gives the outbound departure from Honolua Bay.
nodes.summary: Double-hulled voyaging canoe with cold-molded plywood hulls covered in fiberglass, built for experimental voyaging.
nodes.uncertainty: Modern reconstruction; successful voyages cannot by themselves authenticate every ancient design or migration route. Practice under sail preceded the 1976 research voyage; the anchor is the documented intended project voyage, not a claim that no earlier use occurred.

nodes.title: Hōkūleʻa design study
nodes.date_basis: Low’s participant interview account dates the design project’s start to early 1973; Kāne describes the reasoning retrospectively.
nodes.summary: Kāne and Emory selected widely recorded canoe features as a hypothesis about earlier forms for an experimental vessel.
nodes.uncertainty: Widespread occurrence does not itself prove antiquity. The node records the investigators’ design inference, not its validation.

nodes.title: Hōkūleʻa wayfinding trial
nodes.date_basis: Contemporaneous Kyselka report dates the outward-and-return voyage to March–June 1980.
nodes.summary: Voyage tested learned wayfinding and planetarium-derived cues; estimates were recorded and radioed to an escort for plotting and comparison.
nodes.uncertainty: Participant report, not independent accuracy audit. Escort instrumentation and Mau’s support limit claims of unaided isolation. Ancient navigation is not dated from this experiment.

nodes.title: Jikji metal-type edition
nodes.date_basis: Custodian attributes this surviving volume to Heungdeok-sa printing in 1377.
nodes.summary: Surviving second volume of Jikji, printed using movable cast-metal characters.
nodes.uncertainty: No earliest-ever invention, exact alloy, casting procedure or China/Europe transfer claimed.

nodes.title: Jikji woodblock edition
nodes.date_basis: Custodian identifies the preserved Ch’wi’am xylograph edition as dated 1378.
nodes.summary: Complete text of Jikji in a preserved woodblock edition.
nodes.uncertainty: Same text does not prove that the 1377 metal-type edition supplied the blocks or that one process caused the other.

nodes.title: Korent’s wavefinding demonstration
nodes.date_basis: Original article dates ethnographic fieldwork and observed practice to June 2005–September 2006.
nodes.summary: Korent Joel demonstrated wave-based landfinding during field collaboration, including navigation of a yacht between atolls.
regions: Several atolls including Majuro, Arno and neighboring islands
nodes.uncertainty: The interval dates the demonstration, not the tradition’s origin. Practitioners’ explanations and measured physical mechanisms are kept distinct.

nodes.title: Malindi-assisted ocean passage
nodes.date_basis: Voyage narrative places departure on 24 April, land sighting on 18 May and identification/arrival on 20 May.
nodes.summary: A pilot supplied at Malindi guided Vasco da Gama’s fleet across the Arabian Sea and interpreted coastal landmarks.
regions: Arabian Sea to Calicut/Kozhikode, South Asia
nodes.uncertainty: One narrated application; identity and religious labels are not adopted. No generic astrolabe, compass or Ibn Majid lineage is inferred.

nodes.title: Majuro cross-swell observations
nodes.date_basis: WAM’s participant interview places buoy deployments during the field year beginning in 2005 and culminating in the 2006 voyage; the research paper also states a June 2005–September 2006 fieldwork interval. Exact deployment days are not given.
nodes.summary: Navigator-identified vessel rocking and directional wave measurements were consistent with bent incident swells; multiple wave trains limited field validation.
nodes.uncertainty: The buoy did not resolve claimed reflected signals or dilep. Model agreement at another island is not direct verification of all local cues.

nodes.title: Navigator-guided buoy survey
nodes.date_basis: WAM’s participant interview places buoy deployments during the field year beginning in 2005 and culminating in the 2006 voyage; the research paper also states a June 2005–September 2006 fieldwork interval. Exact deployment days are not given.
nodes.summary: Datawell Directional Waverider G-4 deployments at navigator-selected wave patterns; GPS motion sensing produced directional spectra.
nodes.uncertainty: Exact campaign dates remain unresolved within the stated bounds; the survey is not a universal assessment of wavefinding.

nodes.title: Mau’s Hōkūleʻa navigation
nodes.date_basis: Kyselka’s 1980 account and PVS history date Mau’s guiding voyage to 1976.
nodes.summary: Mau Piailug guided Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti using noninstrument wayfinding.
nodes.uncertainty: 1976 dates this voyage, not the origin of Carolinian knowledge. No sweeping claim that all equipment aboard was nonmodern.

nodes.title: Mau teaches Thompson
nodes.date_basis: Kyselka dates Thompson’s Micronesia visit to March 1979; PVS dates Mau’s return to Hawaiʻi to teach in that year.
nodes.summary: Mau taught Nainoa Thompson and collaborators to integrate wind, waves, swells, birds and stars in wayfinding.
nodes.uncertainty: This is a dated teaching episode, not the first creation or entirety of either community’s knowledge.

nodes.title: Muldoons excavated channel
nodes.date_basis: Rounded combined calibrated ranges of basal infill samples OZL608/OZL760, c. 6450–6740 cal BP (BP=1950), constrain prior excavation. This dates evidence of an existing channel, not its invention.
nodes.summary: Bifurcated channel F10 created by removal of basalt blocks; dated basal infill establishes an earlier excavated form.
nodes.uncertainty: Construction may be older. Charcoal association, old wood and stratigraphic interpretation limit precision; only F10 is represented.

nodes.title: Muldoons channel walls
nodes.date_basis: Article assigns walls to c. 600–800 cal BP; conversion uses BP=1950.
nodes.summary: Multi-tiered basalt walls added along the pre-existing F10 channel.
nodes.uncertainty: A long sedimentary hiatus separates phases; continuous operation or unchanged knowledge transmission is not established.

nodes.title: Planetarium latitude study
nodes.date_basis: The participant account identifies this as preparation already used on the voyage that left on 15 March 1980; the study’s starting date is not established.
nodes.summary: Thompson and Kyselka varied simulated latitude to study star rise/set positions and candidate latitude cues.
nodes.uncertainty: Display date is a by-date for the active method; earlier study duration is not narrowed. No claimed modern priority or accuracy distribution.

nodes.title: Rome’s aqueduct mills
nodes.date_basis: Operational stage at the opening of the 537–538 siege; Procopius’s narrative sequence, with calendar placement checked in Bury.
nodes.summary: Hill mills powered by descending aqueduct water, operating before the siege’s supply cut.
nodes.uncertainty: Procopius says the mills were old; their original construction dates and complete number are not supplied.

nodes.title: Tiber boat mills
nodes.date_basis: Procopius narrates the response at the beginning of the siege; Bury places this episode in 537.
nodes.summary: Customary mill machinery suspended between moored boats, driven by river current below a bridge.
nodes.uncertainty: Literary account; the exact bridge and claims of sufficient flour are not independently verified. Nonmarket is a configuration-specific inference, not evidence of no transactions or a claim about all boat mills.

nodes.title: Protected Tiber mills
nodes.date_basis: Operational stage at the opening of the 537–538 siege; Procopius’s narrative sequence, with calendar placement checked in Bury.
nodes.summary: Operating boat mills accompanied by an upstream iron-chain debris barrier and removal crew.
nodes.uncertainty: Procopius says protection against hostile boats was the stronger motive; this is not a milling-only device.

nodes.title: Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2
nodes.date_basis: Google dates launch to May; 20 May begins contact with sales/partners and a 21 May trade report says partner availability.
nodes.summary: Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2, model GG2; enterprise assisted-reality wearable. Excludes Explorer Edition and Enterprise Edition 1.
nodes.uncertainty: Initial enterprise partner-channel opening is scoped to May 2019. First individual developer direct-reseller purchase came later; any prior private arrangements were not excluded.

nodes.title: Fairchild retained-oxide planar transistor, development
nodes.date_basis: Retrospective identifies Hoerni notebook date.
nodes.summary: The 1957 concept and unnamed 1959 Fairchild working planar prototype; 1959 sample polarity and exact product identity unestablished.
nodes.uncertainty: Do not relabel this research prototype as a confirmed 2N1613 sample.

nodes.title: Intel 4004 microprocessor — merchant non-calculator offer
nodes.date_basis: Intel advertisement reports the MCS-4 family in stock on this day.
nodes.summary: Intel 4004 four-bit CPU, including early development iterations; the commercial event is scoped to Intel merchant sales outside desktop calculators.
nodes.uncertainty: Restricted Busicom contract activity preceded the merchant-market announcement; earliest merchant transaction or earlier private offer has not been independently proved.

nodes.title: Compensating microscope eyepieces
nodes.date_basis: Abbe explains the construction in his 1886 paper; Zeiss retrospectively dates the named eyepiece introduction with the objectives to August 1886.
nodes.summary: Eyepieces deliberately given a color-dependent magnification opposite to the remaining lateral color difference of the objective, so the combined microscope image has less color error away from the axis.
regions: Europe — Zeiss optical works, Jena, Germany
nodes.uncertainty: This specific compensation design is not a claim that eyepiece correction was wholly new. Compatibility depended on objective and eyepiece properties, not the name alone.

nodes.title: Basic Bessemer lining
nodes.date_basis: Blaenavon experiments from 1877, reported success in March 1878, subsequent Middlesbrough refinement in 1879.
nodes.summary: Thomas and Gilchrist modified the converter lining to remove phosphorus during Bessemer steelmaking.
nodes.uncertainty: Heritage account does not specify lining recipe or removal chemistry; those details are withheld.

nodes.title: Belovode copper smelting
nodes.date_basis: Trench 3, occupation horizon D / Gradac phase; archaeological phase range reported by excavators.
nodes.summary: Copper-bearing slag and slagged ceramic sherds document extraction of copper from ore at a Vinča settlement.
nodes.uncertainty: Small debris survives; convincing smelting installations were not identified. This node makes no sole-origin or universal-earliest claim.

nodes.title: Bessemer air conversion
nodes.date_basis: Patent year specified in the Science Museum collection record; not the date of universal commercial reliability.
nodes.summary: Air blown through molten pig iron in a converter; oxidation supplies heat during conversion to steel.
nodes.uncertainty: The object page is retrospective. Its separate compressed statement about later improvements is not used.

nodes.title: Comparative microscope tests
nodes.date_basis: The tests followed the 1886 instrument introductions and preceded Dallinger’s address on 9 February 1887; exact individual test dates are not supplied.
nodes.summary: Dallinger compared Zeiss objectives and compensating eyepieces with his existing high-power lenses, including trials swapping in the new eyepieces; he and Mayall also recorded independent judgments on a supplied series.
regions: Europe — Britain; instruments from Jena and London
nodes.uncertainty: These were reported visual comparisons with selected test objects and high-quality existing lenses, not a modern standardized quantitative trial. Dallinger’s restricted conclusions must not be generalized to all apochromats.

nodes.title: Edsken Bessemer steel
nodes.date_basis: Practical-scale implementation at Edsken dated by the Swedish steel industry historical account.
nodes.summary: Göran Fredrik Göransson applied the Bessemer method on a practical scale and obtained satisfactory steel ingots.
nodes.uncertainty: Institutional retrospective account; its universal-first and sweeping railway claims are not adopted.

nodes.title: Faraday’s heavy optical glass
nodes.date_basis: Faraday dates the dedicated heavy-glass work from September 1828 and describes the established preparation in his lecture read in late 1829.
nodes.summary: Faraday’s silicated borate of lead: a heavy optical glass finished and annealed in platinum trays after purification, mixing and fusion of the constituents.
nodes.uncertainty: The interval dates the reported development of this glass preparation; it does not establish the manufacture date of the particular specimen used in 1845, nor routine commercial optical performance.

nodes.title: Magnetic rotation of polarization
nodes.date_basis: Experiments communicated in a paper received 6 November and read 20 November 1845; publication in 1846 is not used as the event date.
nodes.summary: Polarized light traversing Faraday’s heavy glass along a magnetic field changed its plane of polarization; reversing the magnetic poles reversed the rotation.
nodes.uncertainty: The material was his successful experimental medium, not a universal requirement for the effect; the paper also reports other substances and permanent magnets. This is distinct from mechanical electromagnetic rotation in 1821.

nodes.title: Gerlafingen oxygen converter
nodes.date_basis: ASME history caption dates the experimental top-blown converter to 1948.
nodes.summary: Robert Durrer’s experimental converter applied oxygen from above the iron bath.
nodes.uncertainty: Retrospective landmark account; no commercial Swiss deployment is implied.

nodes.title: Gerzeh meteoritic-iron beads
nodes.date_basis: Closed burials assigned to Naqada IIC–IIIA, approximately 3400–3100 BCE; abstract rounds to 3200 BCE.
nodes.summary: Meteoritic iron hammered into sheet and rolled into tubular beads; a metalworking route requiring no extraction of iron from ore.
nodes.uncertainty: Three museum beads were directly analyzed. The manufacturing sequence is inferred from their structure; no transmission to later iron smelting is asserted.

nodes.title: Great Lakes copper tools
nodes.date_basis: Rounded conversion of the reported 8500–3580 cal BP range for embedded organics, using the 1950 BP epoch; an evidence span, not the lifetime of one culture.
nodes.summary: Large utilitarian tools forged from native copper; dated organic material remains embedded in some copper artifacts.
regions: North America — Lake Superior / western Great Lakes
nodes.uncertainty: Associated organics date use indirectly. Sparse early finds and modeled cultural boundaries must not be equated; no claim of a global first.

nodes.title: Jena optical-glass supply
nodes.date_basis: Abbe’s 1886 report states that the Jena factory had already commenced manufacture for general optical use; this is an attested availability date, not a claim that production began in 1886.
nodes.summary: The Jena Glastechnisches Laboratorium supplied a wider selection of optical glasses, including borate and phosphate compositions with varied refractive-index and dispersion combinations.
nodes.uncertainty: No one universal composition is implied. Earlier prototypes and factory founding are not conflated with this availability endpoint; the exact glass or fluorite content of each objective remains unspecified.

nodes.title: Composition–dispersion experiments
nodes.date_basis: Abbe’s account presented in 1886 explicitly says the Schott–Abbe investigation began in 1881; the interval covers the program reported there.
nodes.summary: Schott and Abbe, with Zeiss workshop cooperation, measured experimental glass melts spectrometrically to relate composition to refractive and dispersive properties and select further compositions.
nodes.uncertainty: The primary report summarizes a multi-year collaboration; it does not date each melt or disclose all optical recipes. The node ends at the 1886 report, not at a claimed termination of research.

nodes.title: Linz oxygen-steel production
nodes.date_basis: Commissioning at Linz on 27 November 1952.
nodes.summary: An operating LD plant converted carbon-rich hot metal into lower-carbon steel by oxygen blowing.
nodes.uncertainty: Developer’s retrospective account; no present-day market-share claim is used.

nodes.title: Linz oxygen-blowing trials
nodes.date_basis: VÖEST chronology: trials began 3 June; changed lance position and pressure on 25 June; larger experimental vessel in October.
nodes.summary: Lower oxygen pressure and a more distant lance yielded steel suitable for rolling into sheet in converter trials.
nodes.uncertainty: Company history reports the result; this node does not attach later production capacity to the trials.

nodes.title: Merv crucible steel
nodes.date_basis: Workshop assigned by the excavators to the ninth–early tenth century; 930 is a display bound for early tenth, not a measured endpoint.
nodes.summary: Workshop crucibles interpreted as evidence for combining cast iron and wrought iron to produce steel.
nodes.uncertainty: Only the abstract was accessible in this pass; detailed context and competing metallurgical interpretations await full-text review.

nodes.title: Pločnik tin-bronze foil
nodes.date_basis: Occupation-horizon date is a terminus ante quem for the foil, not a direct measurement of its manufacture.
nodes.summary: Tin-bronze foil interpreted as metal smelted from complex copper–tin ores, subsequently worked and annealed.
nodes.uncertainty: Ore identification is compositional inference. The broader group contains poorly contextualized finds; the node is restricted to the securely contextualized foil.

nodes.title: Powell–Lealand apochromatic microscope optics
nodes.date_basis: In his address of 9 February 1887 Dallinger recalls the objective and eyepieces displayed at the Society’s November meeting, hence November 1886.
nodes.summary: Powell and Lealand made a 1/12-inch apochromatic objective to their own formula, with compensating eyepieces constructed on Abbe's plan; the combination was exhibited at the Society's November 1886 meeting.
nodes.uncertainty: The account says new glass samples reached English opticians but does not identify Powell and Lealand as recipients or establish which glass they used.

nodes.title: Qiwu’s reported steelmaking
nodes.date_basis: Practice assigned retrospectively to Qiwu Huaiwen in Beishi, chapter 89; this is the reported sixth-century activity, not the later compilation date.
nodes.summary: A biography describes heating powdered cast iron with soft-iron blanks for several days to make steel for sabres.
nodes.uncertainty: Location and exact thermal procedure are uncertain. The modern label co-fusion does not establish that both components melted; the 1955 reconstruction is excluded.

nodes.title: Royal Institution glass furnace
nodes.date_basis: Faraday reports the room and furnaces built in September 1827; the surviving notebook is headed October 1827.
nodes.summary: A dedicated experimental room and furnaces brought Faraday’s optical-glass experiments onto the Royal Institution premises, with Sergeant Anderson assisting.
nodes.uncertainty: This is a particular research installation, not the invention of a glass furnace. The entire manuscript was not inspected.

nodes.title: Zeiss apochromatic objectives
nodes.date_basis: The 1889 manufacturer catalogue dates introduction to August 1886; Abbe’s 1886 report describes their construction and performance aims.
nodes.summary: A manufactured series of microscope objectives using new glass materials and optical formulae, designed to improve chromatic and spherical correction and paired with compensating eyepieces.
regions: Europe — Zeiss optical works, Jena, Germany
nodes.uncertainty: Design and marketing claims are not treated as universal measured superiority. Dallinger’s later comparisons found limits; exact proprietary prescriptions are absent from these passages.

nodes.title: Bronze-and-iron crossbow bolt
nodes.date_basis: Same CB3 attribution as its shaft; these are two production stages evidenced by one object.
nodes.summary: CB3 combines a leaded-bronze head with the treated iron shaft.
regions: East Asia — China, exact findspot unrecorded
nodes.uncertainty: Casting-on is proposed, not directly observed in manufacture.

nodes.title: Cast-and-decarburized iron shaft
nodes.date_basis: CB3 museum attribution: fifth–fourth centuries BCE, Eastern Zhou; manufacture dated by the artifact attribution.
nodes.summary: CB3 shaft: cast to rod shape, then decarburized to low-carbon iron.
regions: East Asia — China, exact findspot unrecorded
nodes.uncertainty: Museum attribution lacks a recorded excavation context; process is inferred from microstructure.

nodes.title: Allen circles of proportion
nodes.date_basis: Whipple catalogue accession 0833 dates the surviving instrument c.1635; decade bounds encode approximate dating, not a measured manufacturing interval.
nodes.summary: Surviving brass circular logarithmic instrument made by Elias Allen to Oughtred's design, using fixed concentric scales and paired radial index arms.
nodes.uncertainty: Approximate museum dating. It is a surviving object, not evidence that the form was first conceived in 1635.

nodes.title: Brahmagupta zero rules
nodes.date_basis: Composition date supplied by the edited-text header; the surviving editions and translation are much later.
nodes.summary: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta chapter 18 treats positive, negative and zero quantities in addition, subtraction and multiplication; a multiplied quantity times zero gives zero.
nodes.uncertainty: Not an origin claim for zero notation. The division statements include zero divided by zero as zero; this is not a modern field-arithmetic rule. No direct transmission to a named Arabic text is established here.

nodes.title: Briggs common logarithms
nodes.date_basis: Publication of Logarithmorum Chilias Prima in London after the 1615–1616 discussions with Napier.
nodes.summary: Published common-logarithm tables following discussion and revision of Napier's scheme; the node is the 1617 publication, not sole attribution of the idea.
nodes.uncertainty: Briggs credited Napier for the useful normalization; the concept and numerical labour should not be assigned to a single inventor.

nodes.title: Bugia numeral instruction
nodes.date_basis: Leonardo retrospectively places this in his childhood before composing Liber abaci. Lower bound uses the approximate 1170 birth date; 1190 is only a display anchor, not an attested lesson date.
nodes.summary: Leonardo Pisano reports receiving instruction in calculation with the nine Indian figures while his father served the Pisan merchant community at Bugia.
nodes.uncertainty: This is autobiographical testimony preserved in the revised work. The teacher's identity, exact year, language and ethnic identity are not supplied and are not guessed.

nodes.title: Dutch spyglass demonstrated
nodes.date_basis: Lipperhey's demonstration and the States General record of 2 October 1608; does not date a unique invention event.
nodes.summary: A working distance-magnifying spyglass presented by Hans Lipperhey and recorded in a patent request; other maker claims remain distinct.
nodes.uncertainty: The record supports presentation, not exclusive inventorship; no particular later specimen is claimed to be this instrument.

nodes.title: Galileo astronomical telescopes
nodes.date_basis: Construction and improvement ran from 1609 into early 1610; lunar and planetary observing configurations were attained at different points.
nodes.summary: Galileo's progressively improved convex-objective/concave-eyepiece telescopes, with selected or manufactured lenses adequate for his lunar and later planetary observations.
nodes.uncertainty: A sequence of instruments, not one unchanged telescope. Claimed thirty-power performance is not adopted as a measured specification of the discovery instrument.

nodes.title: Jupiter satellites tracked
nodes.date_basis: Dated observations begin 7 January; four objects are recorded on 13 January; interpretation follows the changing positions.
nodes.summary: Repeated telescopic positions of objects near Jupiter, interpreted as four bodies revolving around it rather than fixed stars.
nodes.uncertainty: Priority disputes with other observers are not resolved here; the result alone does not distinguish every geocentric, geoheliocentric and heliocentric system.

nodes.title: Lunar relief observed
nodes.date_basis: Museo Galileo dates the surviving Moon drawings to November–December 1609; the interpretation was published in 1610.
nodes.summary: Repeated telescopic views of the lunar light-shadow boundary and isolated illuminated features interpreted as an uneven surface with elevations and depressions.
nodes.uncertainty: This is Galileo's observation programme, not the first human telescopic look at the Moon; the inference is distinct from a direct topographic survey.

nodes.title: Gunter logarithmic scale
nodes.date_basis: Retrospective museum date for introduction of logarithmic rules used with dividers, not a dated surviving specimen.
nodes.summary: A physical logarithmically divided rule on which a pair of dividers transfers distances to calculate.
nodes.uncertainty: The date relies on a museum synthesis. The separate 1623 cross-staff proposal in Whipple's catalogue is not conflated with this rule or used as an exact construction date.

nodes.title: Al-Hawari worked arithmetic
nodes.date_basis: The work states completion on 18 Dhu al-Qaʿda 704 AH, interpreted by the editors as 12 June 1305 Julian; surviving copies are later.
nodes.summary: Worked computational illustrations of Ibn al-Banna's rules, including 4043 + 2685 = 6728 with a zero place and explicit carrying between ranks.
nodes.uncertainty: The 2021 translation normalizes figures for reading; original manuscript glyph forms should be checked separately before drawing a paleographic lineage. Worked examples are not proof of population-wide adoption.

nodes.title: Ibn al-Banna arithmetic rules
nodes.date_basis: The critical edition says shortly before 1301; 1256 is the author's birth and only a conservative lower bound. The anchor near 1300 is approximate, not an attested composition year.
nodes.summary: Condensed Book on the Operations of Arithmetic gives rules for known and unknown quantities, including place-aligned addition, without worked numerical examples.
nodes.uncertainty: No invention claim for the rules. Dating is a terminus before 1301; the wide interval encodes limited evidence rather than continuous development over the author's life.

nodes.title: Al-Khwarizmi numeral algorithms
nodes.date_basis: Folkerts places composition in the first half of the ninth century in Baghdad; 825 is a conventional midpoint, not an exact dated manuscript.
nodes.summary: Arithmetic procedures using nine numeral signs and decimal places, with a small circle for an empty place, attributed to Indian reckoning in the later Latin textual tradition.
nodes.uncertainty: The Arabic original and original Arabic title are lost. Details are reconstructed through Latin redactions, not directly read from an Arabic ninth-century manuscript; no particular Sanskrit source is identified.

nodes.title: Latin Dixit Algorizmi
nodes.date_basis: Folkerts dates the Latin translation and redaction to the twelfth century; the anchor is a display midpoint. Surviving manuscript copies are later.
nodes.summary: Latin reworking of al-Khwarizmi-derived arithmetic, preserving decimal positions, nine numeral signs and a small-circle placeholder; includes operational arithmetic rules.
regions: Latin Europe; translation probably in Iberia
nodes.uncertainty: Cambridge Ii.6.5 and New York HC 397/726 preserve differing revisions, not the lost first translation. Neither a named translator nor Toledo is asserted as settled.

nodes.title: Latin Liber Alchorismi
nodes.date_basis: Folkerts groups the work among twelfth-century Latin adaptations; no exact composition year is established.
nodes.summary: A separate Latin arithmetic exposition expanding and arranging al-Khwarizmi-derived calculation methods, including operations on integers and fractions and square-root extraction.
nodes.uncertainty: The magister Iohannes named as author is not securely identified with John of Seville. The precise relation and order of Liber Alchorismi and Liber pulveris are not resolved here.

nodes.title: Liber abaci positional arithmetic
nodes.date_basis: Dates the surviving revised work, not the lost first redaction of 1202 or the date of its later manuscript copies.
nodes.summary: The revised Liber abaci teaches writing numbers with nine figures plus 0, decimal place values and explicit empty-place examples such as 209, alongside arithmetic procedures.
nodes.uncertainty: The opening heading recalls 1202, but surviving content must not automatically be assigned to that lost first version. No broad merchant adoption is inferred from the text's existence.

nodes.title: Napier logarithms
nodes.date_basis: Publication of Mirifici logarithmorum canonis descriptio; not the beginning of Napier's decades of work.
nodes.summary: Published logarithmic calculation and tables, in Napier's original normalization rather than modern base-10 form.
nodes.uncertainty: No universal priority asserted; independent logarithmic developments are outside this first batch.

nodes.title: Differential refraction experiments
nodes.date_basis: Newton's 1672 paper retrospectively dates the initial prism investigations to the beginning of 1666; not contemporaneous publication.
nodes.summary: Prism investigations leading Newton to identify differing refrangibility among components of sunlight and to diagnose a limitation of simple refracting objectives.
nodes.uncertainty: The chronology is Newton's later account. No endorsement of his broader claim that refracting telescopes could never overcome colour error.

nodes.title: Newton reflecting telescope
nodes.date_basis: Museo Galileo dates the first construction to 1668; Newton's 1672 account distinguishes it from the later instrument sent to London.
nodes.summary: A telescope Newton built with a polished metal reflecting objective, avoiding refraction at the objective; distinct from the later Royal Society instrument.
nodes.uncertainty: No unique invention claim; Gregory's 1663 reflecting design is a separate earlier proposal. The generic modern parabolic specification is not imposed on Newton's first mirror.

nodes.title: Oughtred sliding scales
nodes.date_basis: Whipple dates the attributed sliding-scale invention only to the 1620s; the anchor is a display midpoint, not a documented year.
nodes.summary: Two Gunter-type logarithmic scales moved alongside one another so their relative displacement replaces transfer with dividers.
nodes.uncertainty: Approximate retrospective attribution; this node does not equate an early conception, a 1632 description, and a surviving instrument.

nodes.title: Al-Uqlidisi board reckoning
nodes.date_basis: Composition of Chapters on Indian Arithmetic in Damascus, dated 341 AH; this is a textual attestation, not the invention of board calculation.
nodes.summary: The erasable-board arithmetic taken as the starting configuration in al-Uqlidisi's treatment: digits and intermediate results can be erased or shifted during calculation.
nodes.uncertainty: No preserved tenth-century board is claimed. This node dates the described practice in the book, not its first regional use.

nodes.title: Al-Uqlidisi paper algorithms
nodes.date_basis: Book IV of the work composed in 341 AH; the date belongs to the description rather than demonstrated widespread adoption.
nodes.summary: Pen-and-paper calculation procedures avoiding the earlier erasure operation; one described multiplication combines Indian operand digits with abjad-written intermediate products.
nodes.uncertainty: The passage describes a method, not universal displacement of dust boards or invention of paper. Abjad and Indian signs coexisted; the book is not a simple replacement story.

nodes.title: Bersham cylinder boring
nodes.date_basis: Bounded by large-cylinder supply ordered in June 1775 for the engine operating in March 1776; the exact commissioning date of the illustrated machine is not established.
nodes.summary: Wilkinson's large-cylinder machining: a stationary cylinder secured on its bed and a rotating boring bar supported beyond both ends, with the cutter fed along the bar.
nodes.uncertainty: The 1775–76 dating attaches securely to the output/supply episode; association with the exact reconstructed machine is less secure. Gilpin's original plan was not independently inspected. Museum loading details, works-founding date and universal priority claims are excluded.

nodes.title: Bloomfield pumping engine
nodes.date_basis: Engine start reported in Aris's Birmingham Gazette, 11 March 1776, as identified by the archive and technical history.
nodes.summary: Boulton & Watt's single-acting mine-pumping engine at Bloomfield, with a 50-inch cylinder ordered from Wilkinson in June 1775.
nodes.uncertainty: The cited newspaper and original order were not separately retrieved. This is not claimed to be the first steam engine or the origin of every later engine.

nodes.title: Carnot’s heat-engine analysis
nodes.date_basis: Publication of Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu, Paris, Bachelier.
nodes.summary: A reversible-cycle argument that, for a given quantity of caloric transferred, the maximum obtainable work depends on the reservoir temperatures rather than the working substance, developed while examining existing heat engines and their improvement.
nodes.uncertainty: Carnot's published argument uses conserved caloric. It is not the modern energy-conservation formulation or a claim that he supplied an already implemented engine design. Inspected passages, not the entire book.

nodes.title: Clapeyron’s analytic heat cycle
nodes.date_basis: Original memoir in Journal de l'École polytechnique, tome XIV, cahier XXIII, pp. 153–190; date confirmed by BnF record.
nodes.summary: Clapeyron explicitly takes Carnot's reasoning as his starting point and expresses cycle work through pressure–volume geometry and mathematical analysis.
nodes.uncertainty: The early caloric framework is retained; this node is not the complete modern second law. Original French pp. 153–157 read in scan/OCR; p. 155 visually verified. English 1837 translation passages were also consulted.

nodes.title: Clausius’s heat-work reconciliation
nodes.date_basis: Communicated in Berlin in February 1850 and published in parts during 1850; English translation 1851, collected edition 1867. No exact publication month is required here.
nodes.summary: Clausius combined equivalence of heat and work with a modified Carnot argument: part of the heat can be converted to work while another part passes from a warmer body to a colder one.
nodes.uncertainty: Read in the 1867 English collection. Bracketed 1864 additions are excluded. The 1850 node is not the later naming of entropy; other contributors and parallel approaches remain outside this subset.

nodes.title: Separate condenser model
nodes.date_basis: Museum attribution of surviving object 1876-1267; this is a model date, not industrial operation.
nodes.summary: Watt's surviving second cylinder-and-separate-condenser model; condensation occurs outside the working cylinder.
nodes.uncertainty: Formerly misidentified as the first model. The museum describes alterations and probable sealing difficulties; reliable prolonged operation is not claimed.

nodes.title: Separate condenser specification
nodes.date_basis: Patent dated 5 January; specification enrolled 29 April 1769.
nodes.summary: Watt's specification couples a hot, insulated steam vessel to a separately cooled condenser and provides for pumps to remove air or other uncondensed elastic vapour.
nodes.uncertainty: The museum catalogue of the original document was inspected; its document images were not transcribed independently. Patent coverage is not evidence of operation.

nodes.title: Double-acting steam specification
nodes.date_basis: Patent granted 12 March; specification enrolled 4 July 1782.
nodes.summary: Watt describes alternating steam admission and condensation above and below the piston, transmitting both push and pull through rack-and-sector or other connections.
nodes.uncertainty: A patent describes claimed arrangements; it does not alone establish operation or the stated doubling of actual output.

nodes.title: Expansive steam specification
nodes.date_basis: Patent granted 12 March; specification enrolled 4 July 1782.
nodes.summary: Watt specifies cutting off admission during the stroke and using steam expansion for the remainder, with a quarter-stroke example and an approximate pressure/work calculation.
nodes.uncertainty: This node dates the specification, not first conception or first use. Its inverse-volume steam-pressure approximation is historical, not adopted as a generally correct steam model.

nodes.title: Joule’s early heat equivalent
nodes.date_basis: July 1843 dated paper; August presentation and later 1843 serial publication, distinguished from the 1884 collected edition.
nodes.summary: Joule compared mechanical expenditure with heating in magneto-electric experiments, reporting an initial mean equivalent of 838 foot-pounds per pound of water warmed by one Fahrenheit degree, while acknowledging substantial scatter.
nodes.uncertainty: 838 is the historical reported estimate, not the accepted modern equivalent. The claim of reverse convertibility goes beyond a direct demonstration in every stated case.

nodes.title: Precision friction calorimeter
nodes.date_basis: Apparatus documented in the paper dated 4 June, received 6 June and read 21 June 1849; printed in 1850. Manufacture and individual trial dates are not supplied.
nodes.summary: Falling weights drove paddle wheels in calorimetric vessels. Dancer and Fastré thermometers, calibrated using Regnault’s method, measured small rises; separate trials estimated heat leakage, apparatus heat capacity, pulley friction and residual motion.
nodes.uncertainty: The apparatus is dated by its 1849 report. Thermometer readability is not treated as absolute accuracy; the full error budget has not been independently recalculated.

nodes.title: Joule’s refined heat equivalent
nodes.date_basis: Paper dated 4 June, received 6 June, read 21 June 1849; 1850 is its journal publication year.
nodes.summary: Water, mercury and cast-iron friction series compared expended mechanical work with corrected heating. Joule preferred the water result 772.692 foot-pounds and rounded his conclusion to 772 per pound of water warmed by 1 °F near 55–60 °F.
nodes.uncertainty: Historical result and thermal reference conditions are retained. No claim that the last digits represent modern accuracy; Joule explicitly notes residual vibration and sound.

nodes.title: Magneto-electric calorimeter
nodes.date_basis: The paper is signed July 1843 and was read at Cork on 21 August 1843; dates the reported apparatus, not an independently established construction day.
nodes.summary: Joule rotated a compound electromagnet immersed in water between magnetic poles, measured circuit current with a galvanometer, and measured water-temperature change; the initial inducing magnets were reused from an electromagnetic engine.
regions: Broom Hill, Pendlebury, near Manchester, England
nodes.uncertainty: Configurations changed across experiments. This node describes the initial calorimetric arrangement, not every later trial or a modern efficiency claim.

nodes.title: Joule’s revised magnetocalorimeter
nodes.date_basis: The 1843 report distinguishes the new inducing magnet before series 2 and its later repeated use with weights; no exact trial day is assigned.
nodes.summary: Joule reused the immersed rotating electromagnet with a newly built stationary inducing magnet in the later series 2 arrangement, then repeated that series with falling weights when estimating the 1843 heat equivalent.
regions: Broom Hill, Pendlebury, near Manchester, England
nodes.uncertainty: This is the specifically revised series 2 configuration, not a claim that the initial engine-magnet arrangement remained unchanged.

nodes.title: Papplewick mill engine drawing
nodes.date_basis: Repository dates the surviving elevation to 1785; this is not used as a precise commissioning date.
nodes.summary: Boulton & Watt elevation of the Robinson cotton mill showing an 11-horsepower sun-and-planet engine with 17½-inch cylinder and four-foot stroke, alongside evidence of the earlier waterwheel.
nodes.uncertainty: The catalogue supplies the installation interpretation and dimensions; the original-resolution drawing was not inspected in this batch. No cotton-industry priority claim or exact operating start is adopted.

nodes.title: Regnault’s steam measurements
nodes.date_basis: First published volume of the government-commissioned Relation des expériences, as identified contemporaneously by Thomson. Individual measurement dates are not assigned.
nodes.summary: Published measurements of saturated-steam pressure and latent heat per unit mass, undertaken for steam-engine calculations; Thomson describes the published range as 0–230 °C and the missing density information needed for his calculations.
nodes.uncertainty: The recipient’s contemporary account and bibliographic record were inspected; Regnault’s underlying experimental volume was not retrieved (Gallica 403). No claim of auditing its apparatus or tables.

nodes.title: Sun-and-planet specification
nodes.date_basis: Patent granted 25 October 1781; detailed specification signed 13 February and enrolled 23 February 1782.
nodes.summary: Watt's fifth patented method converts reciprocating engine motion into continuous shaft rotation with sun-and-planet gearing; the specification also describes an internal-tooth variant.
nodes.uncertainty: The primary specification was read in a web transcription of a scholarly documentary edition. Its OCR errors and intermediate hosting are recorded; invention priority between Watt and Murdock is not asserted.

nodes.title: Cannon-friction heat apparatus
nodes.date_basis: Dates the experimental report read 25 January 1798, not the construction or first observation. Exact experiment dates are not established here.
nodes.summary: Rumford adapted a brass cannon end into a hollow cylinder, rotated by horse-driven boring machinery against a blunt tool; a thermometer and surrounding water registered frictional heating.
nodes.uncertainty: The report is evidence of the described experiment, not a calibrated modern heat/work measurement. No Wilkinson-to-Munich transmission or immediate overthrow of caloric theory is claimed.

nodes.title: Steam-powered engine-shop tools
nodes.date_basis: Conversion occurred after the engine's 1783 corn-mill use and before its dismantling in 1803. Anchor 1793 is the interval midpoint for layout, not a claimed conversion year.
nodes.summary: The same Soho double-reciprocating engine was subsequently applied to lathes and drills in the engine shops; Southern called it the boring engine.
nodes.uncertainty: The conversion year, individual tools, and products made with them are not identified. No arrow back to the earlier Wilkinson machine is asserted.

nodes.title: Soho double-acting engine
nodes.date_basis: First drawing dated August 1782; operation appears in a March 1783 diary reference, while the engine list gives first trial in June 1783.
nodes.summary: An 18-inch-cylinder, double-acting rotative engine using rack-and-sector connection and internal sun-and-planet gear, initially driving a corn mill.
nodes.uncertainty: Item-level catalogue inspected, not all drawings or diary leaves. The catalogue notes conflicting stroke lengths and first-operation records; no precise stroke or month is asserted.

nodes.title: Soho engine trials
nodes.date_basis: Trials reported in connection with the April 1775 replacement-cylinder correspondence and subsequent commercial supply.
nodes.summary: Watt's relocated experimental engine, rebuilt with Wilkinson's replacement cylinder and smaller parts made by Soho craftsmen, underwent promising trials.
nodes.uncertainty: No measured test-series results are available in these inspected passages; successful trials are a historian's account, not a performance dataset.

nodes.title: Thomson’s first absolute scale
nodes.date_basis: October 1848 Philosophical Magazine, vol. 33, pp. 313–317. This dates the published proposal.
nodes.summary: A thermometric scale in which a unit of heat descending through any one degree yields the same mechanical effect, constructed from Carnot-style reasoning and an approximate use of Regnault’s steam data.
nodes.uncertainty: This caloric-based 1848 proposal is not the later linear Kelvin scale. Thomson still expresses doubt about heat/work conversion and lacks reliable saturated-vapour densities across the full range.

nodes.title: Thomson’s Carnot calculations
nodes.date_basis: Explicit read date printed with the original account; distinct from the later appendix.
nodes.summary: On 2 January 1849 Thomson presented an account using Regnault’s steam observations, discussing Joule while provisionally retaining caloric conservation. In an appendix read 30 April 1849, he compared Regnault-derived values with Carnot’s and Clapeyron’s earlier results.
nodes.uncertainty: Later bracketed notes in the collected edition are excluded from the 1849 proposition. Quoting Carnot does not by itself establish physical access to a particular copy.

nodes.title: Thomson’s dynamical heat theory
nodes.date_basis: Read 17 March 1851; original Transactions volume is dated 1853, and a Philosophical Magazine reprint appeared in 1852. This node dates the presentation.
nodes.summary: Thomson explicitly combined Joule’s equivalence principle, reversible-engine reasoning attributed to Carnot and Clausius, and Regnault-based numerical results to construct a dynamical account of heat-engine performance.
nodes.uncertainty: Thomson says his own proof preceded learning Clausius’s proof; acknowledgment is not treated as evidence that Clausius caused its invention. Historical thermal-unit conventions are not silently normalized.

nodes.title: Wilkinson’s trial cylinder
nodes.date_basis: Boulton's 24 April 1775 letter is identified in the technical history; the order was already under discussion in January.
nodes.summary: An approximately 18-inch replacement cylinder machined by John Wilkinson and supplied for Watt's experimental engine at Soho.
nodes.uncertainty: The actual machine used for this small cylinder is not securely identified. Andrew proposes a rotating-workpiece cannon-boring machine as a likelihood; that conjecture is not adopted as fact.

nodes.date_basis: The 22 July 1969 participant interview reports departure from Safi on May 25.
